title: Senate Unveils CLARITY Act Text With Developer Safe Harbor and Ethics Sunset
excerpt: Senate Republicans released the long-awaited crypto market structure bill on Wednesday, preserving Section 604 protections for non-custodial software developers while banning officials from sponsoring digital assets until January 2029.
body:
• The Digital Asset Market Clarity Act divides oversight of digital assets between the SEC and CFTC.
  • An ethics provision prohibits certain political officials from engaging in digital asset activities until January 2029.
  • The bill provides a safe harbor for developers of non-custodial software, exempting them from being classified as money transmitters.
  • Crypto companies can raise up to $50 million annually without SEC registration, limiting regulatory scrutiny on token sales.

Senate Republicans on Wednesday unveiled the text of the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, the landmark crypto legislation that would divide oversight of digital assets between the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The release ends weeks of delay over an ethics provision tied to President Donald Trump's crypto business interests, according to Reuters.

The bill preserves Section 604 — known as the Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act (BRCA) — which creates a statutory safe harbor for developers who publish or maintain non-custodial software. Under the provision, developers who do not control user funds cannot be classified as money transmitters under the Bank Secrecy Act or prosecuted under the criminal money transmission statute.

What the Bill Contains

The released text covers six major areas. The ethics provision bans certain political officials — including the president, vice president, and some members of Congress — from issuing or sponsoring a digital asset until January 2029. Enforcement falls to the Department of Justice, not state attorneys general, a point that has drawn immediate pushback from Democrats.

https://x.com/BTCNewsGlobal/status/2079535220504551912

Senator Angela Alsobrooks has called DOJ enforcement "unserious," given that Trump's former personal lawyer Todd Blanche is the current nominee to head the department. The bill explicitly bars state attorneys general from bringing enforcement cases.

"The administration is committed to working with Congress to see the CLARITY Act advance and has agreed to the most comprehensive and wide-ranging ethics provision in history."

— White House official, in a statement

On stablecoins, the bill bans rewards on idle balances but permits them for transaction-based activity. Crypto companies would be allowed to raise up to $50 million per year — and $200 million in total — without SEC registration, sharply limiting the regulator's ability to treat token sales as illegal securities offerings. The bill also defines when a decentralized platform must comply with bank-like anti-money-laundering rules.

The Developer Safe Harbor

Section 604 was among the most contested provisions in the months leading up to the text's release. A coalition of law enforcement organizations, including the National Sheriffs' Association and the National District Attorneys Association, had urged the administration to strip the provision, arguing it could create gaps in anti-money-laundering oversight.

Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) countered with a formal letter on July 7, demanding the safe harbor remain intact. "Developers who make and release software that allows people to manage their own digital assets — and, critically, where the developer does not control user assets — should not be treated as money transmitters solely because they create or publish software," Wyden wrote.

More than 60 crypto industry CEOs — from Coinbase, a16z crypto, Uniswap, Solana Labs, Kraken, and Paradigm — had signed a letter calling the BRCA a non-negotiable condition of their support. The provision is a direct response to the prosecution of Tornado Cash developer Roman Storm, which established that publishing non-custodial software does not shield developers from criminal charges.

The Political Math

The bill needs at least eight Democratic votes to clear the Senate's 60-vote filibuster threshold. The House passed its version 294 to 134 in July 2025, and the Senate Banking Committee advanced its text 15 to 9 on May 14, 2026, with Senators Ruben Gallego (D-AZ) and Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD) providing the only Democratic support.

Both senators conditioned their floor votes on strong ethics language. Whether the DOJ-only enforcement model satisfies enough Democrats remains the central question. Polymarket odds of the CLARITY Act becoming law in 2026 jumped from 32% to about 43% after the ethics deal was first reported on July 20, but those odds were set before Democrats saw the actual text released today.

Coinbase vice chair Ryan VanGrack told CNBC that Democrats used the negotiations to strengthen customer protections. "At the end of the day, this is about customer protections," VanGrack said. "The Democrats used this opportunity, wisely, to make sure that customers were first and foremost in this bill."

Why Indian-Origin Developers Should Pay Attention

India hosts the world's second-largest crypto developer community, accounting for 11.8% of the global Web3 workforce, according to the India Web3 Landscape Report. The country added 4.7 million Web3 developers to GitHub in 2024, with 85% of new entrants under the age of 27. Indian-origin founders have built globally prominent projects including Polygon and FalconX, and an estimated 60% of Indian Web3 startups are registered abroad but hire technical talent from India.

For the thousands of Indian-origin developers working in the US — building DeFi applications, contributing to open-source protocols, or shipping self-custody wallet software — the CLARITY Act's safe harbor would replace legal ambiguity with clear statutory protection. Without it, developers remain one enforcement action away from prosecution in the same legal gray zone that ensnared the Tornado Cash and Samourai Wallet cases, while competing jurisdictions like Singapore, Dubai, and the EU under MiCA actively court the talent the US risks losing.

What Comes Next

The Senate has until August 7 — the last session day before the summer recess — to bring the bill to a floor vote. If it passes, the legislation returns to the House, which is out of session until September, for approval of any changes before reaching the president's desk. The compressed timeline leaves little room for the kind of prolonged debate that could unravel the fragile bipartisan consensus behind the bill.
